name: TCA peel
lead: A TCA peel is a chemical peel using trichloroacetic acid, generally classed as medium depth and performed in a clinic or surgical setting by a medical provider.[1] The acid coagulates skin proteins, causing controlled necrosis of the epidermis and upper dermis, followed by shedding and collagen remodelling.[2]

TCA at roughly 10 to 50 percent is used for resurfacing in acne scars, fine wrinkles and photoaging, while stronger concentrations are used on individual lesions such as warts.[2] German dermatologist Paul Unna reported its use in peels in 1882.[2]

The published literature includes many small clinical studies and technique papers, covering photoaging, melasma, atrophic acne scars and pigmented lesions. In July 2024 the US FDA warned against using certain TCA peel products without professional supervision because of burn and scarring risks.[2]

paras: Studies and registered trials have examined TCA peels for photoaged skin and actinic keratoses,[3] atrophic acne scars,[4] melasma,[5] benign pigmented lesions in darker skin,[6] and hand lentigines.[7]

Because penetration of TCA varies, authors have described combination methods intended to make depth more predictable: Jessner's solution followed by TCA,[3][8] 70% glycolic acid followed by 35% TCA,[9] and a standardized TCA-based Blue Peel with depth control.[10] Pretreatment with tretinoin was reported in a randomized study to accelerate healing after TCA peeling.[11] Other trials compare TCA with fractional laser or microneedling.[12]

Chemical peels as a group are associated with photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia and textural change, with complications rising with depth; medium peels cause warmth or burning and clinicians may use oral analgesics or topical anesthetics.[1] A comparison of two topical anesthetics for medium-depth peeling was published in 2000.[13] Concentrated TCA is classed as causing severe skin burns and scarring, and China has prohibited it as a cosmetic ingredient.[2] Authors of a 2017 paper noted that fear of pigmentary complications and scarring leads many physicians to avoid TCA peels in darker skin, and described a technique intended for light and dark skin.[14]

A 1989 report described the Jessner's + TCA peel as effective for photoaging, actinic keratoses and wrinkles.[3] A double-blind study in 16 older men found tretinoin pretreatment accelerated healing after a 35% TCA peel.[11] A 2014 study of 50 patients with atrophic acne scars combined subcision, microneedling and 15% TCA peel.[4] Comparative studies have examined TCA with ascorbic acid for melasma.[5] Registered trials compare TCA with Jessner's solution for melasma,[15] with fractional laser,[12] and with intralesional saline for acne scars.[16] Many studies are small and use differing protocols.

Do-it-yourself TCA peeling has been discussed on looksmax.org, where at least one thread asks members about home application. The FDA warning above concerns unsupervised use of certain products. No published studies have examined home application by non-professionals.

card.summary: A medium-depth acid peel with decades of small clinical studies for scars, pigment and photoaging, and a real burn and scarring risk when done wrongly.
card.note: FDA warned in 2024 against certain TCA peel products used without professional supervision.

quick.overview:
A TCA peel applies trichloroacetic acid to the face to cause controlled injury, so damaged outer skin sheds and new skin forms. It is used for photoaging, acne scars and pigment.

Studies are mostly small, but the technique has been described in the literature since the 1980s.
quick.mechanism: TCA coagulates skin proteins in the epidermis and upper dermis, followed by shedding and collagen remodelling.
quick.risks: Redness, crusting, pigment change and scarring are documented; the FDA issued a warning in 2024 about unsupervised use of certain products.
